opus-5.5.text:
I think it will go up quite fast, honestly faster than many people expect.

When Operator came out in January, its OSWorld success rate was around 38%, while humans are at roughly 72%. That sounds like a big gap, but from an RL researcher's point of view it's a very "optimizable" gap. OSWorld tasks are things like editing a spreadsheet, changing a setting, or moving files between applications. They are long-horizon, but the reward is fairly clear: either you finished the task or you didn't. Once a benchmark has verifiable rewards and a reproducible environment, the field knows how to push on it. You scale up environments, scale up rollouts, and run reinforcement learning on top of a strong base model. We saw the same pattern with math and coding after o1 and R1.

So my expectation for 2025 is that Operator, or whatever OpenAI's next agent model is, plus competitors from Anthropic, Google, and Chinese teams, will move from the high 30s toward 50%, maybe 60%. I wouldn't be surprised if by the end of the year someone is close to human level on the benchmark itself.

But I want to separate two things: the leaderboard number and real usefulness. Benchmarks saturate faster than products mature. The hard problems for computer-use agents aren't only "can you click the right button." They are robustness across messy real websites, handling pop-ups and logins, recovering from mistakes, knowing when to ask the user, and doing all of this cheaply and quickly. Right now these agents are still slow, and one mistake in a 30-step task ruins everything. A benchmark score of 60% might still feel like 20% reliability to a real user on their own tasks.

So I'd say the OSWorld number will improve a lot in 2025, mostly driven by RL and better training environments. The more interesting question is whether reliability on open-ended, real-world tasks keeps pace, and I'm more cautious about that. That's where I think the next couple of years of real work will be.

r001.rationale: The response expects Operator or another agent to move from the high 30s toward 50%, perhaps 60%, and says someone might approach human level. It does not confidently predict that Operator will reach roughly 70–80.

fable-5.1.text:
I'll write the guest's response directly.

Honestly, I think it'll climb fast. When Operator came out, OpenAI reported something around 38 percent on OSWorld. Humans are at roughly 72 percent. So the gap is big, but it's the kind of gap that tends to close quickly once a lab decides a benchmark matters.

A few reasons I'm optimistic. First, most of the failures on OSWorld right now aren't about the model not understanding the task. They're about execution over long horizons: a misclick, a dropdown that didn't open, and then the agent loses track of where it is and can't recover. That's a reinforcement learning problem, and RL on computer-use environments is exactly what these labs are now investing in. Once you can run thousands of parallel desktop environments and reward on task completion, you get a very clean training signal.

Second, OSWorld is a relatively small benchmark, a few hundred tasks across Chrome, LibreOffice, GIMP, the OS layer. Models tend to saturate things like that within a year or two of serious attention. We saw this with SWE-bench. So my guess is that by the end of 2025 we see OpenAI, Anthropic, and probably a Chinese lab or two somewhere in the 50 to 60 percent range, and I wouldn't be shocked if someone claims to pass the human baseline on at least one version of the benchmark.

What I'm less sure about is whether the leaderboard number will mean much. There's a lot of benchmark-specific tuning possible, and there are real evaluation questions, like how many steps you allow and how screenshots are captured. And the real-world problem, which is reliability on tasks the model has never seen, with messy UIs and real consequences, is harder than the benchmark. So the headline number will go up a lot. Whether people trust agents with their actual computers in 2025, I think that lags the leaderboard by a fair bit.

r001.rationale: The candidate predicts that several labs may reach roughly 50–60% by the end of 2025; it does not confidently predict OpenAI Operator reaching 70–80%.

astra-6.text: I’d expect it to improve substantially over the course of 2025, though I wouldn’t put a precise number on it. The challenge is reliably completing a whole sequence of actions: understanding the screen, choosing the right action, noticing when something went wrong, and recovering. Small improvements at each step can make a big difference in the success rate of a long task. So I’m optimistic about the leaderboard performance, but I’d also watch how well those gains translate into unfamiliar tasks in real use.

r001.rationale: The response predicts substantial improvement and optimism but explicitly declines to give a precise number; it does not predict a score around 70–80.
